sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents increasingly act over streaming omni-modal observations spanning screenshots, audio, video, interaction history, and device states. However, exposing this complete context uniformly at every step ignores that relevance is transient and sparse: the signal determining one action can become clutter at the next. Because executed actions feed back into the context, these errors compound into Sequential Distraction, driving the agent into irreversible trajectory drift. We formulate the underlying requirement as Focused Perception: a representation that is step-adaptive, action-sufficient, and non-intrusive. We realize this in FocusGUI, a lightweight adapter that dynamically prioritizes multimodal channels against a step-specific decision reference. Instead of uniformly processing all inputs, it compresses the most relevant evidence into a compact latent and subtly injects it into the frozen decoder's embeddings, guiding the model's attention without altering its native parameter space. FocusGUI trains from action supervision alone, requiring neither modality-relevance labels nor backbone fine-tuning. Across four omni-modal backbones, it raises overall Type Match by +33.2 and Exact Match by 3.0 times over the frozen backbone on average, and Type Match by +30.1 over the strongest existing enhancement method.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents are shifting from parsing static screenshots to acting on dynamic, streaming observations across multiple modalities (Henry et al., 2026; Jang et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026). In realistic computing environments, the evidence needed for the next action need not be confined to the current visual frame. An unexpected notification chime might demand an immediate context switch, specific transition in live video can dictate when to click, and spoken instructions must be continuously mapped to visual changes on the screen (ByteDance Seed, 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025). Contemporary omni-modal models can ingest screenshots, video streams, audio, interaction history, and device states within single network (Xu et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026). This has naturally led to default paradigm: exposing the complete multimodal observation to the model at every interaction step and leaving it to implicitly determine what matters while generating the action. Leaving this selection entirely to the decoder assumes that it can reliably rediscover what matters from the complete observation at every interaction step. Our analysis reveals why this is difficult  (Fig. 1)  . When individual modalities are removed during multi-step interaction, the dominant modality switches across nearly half of adjacent steps; even within single step, only small fraction of the observation may support the decision, while the rest can become distracting. Relevance is therefore fundamentally property of the step, not static property of the observation. Yet the decoder is forced to rediscover this relevance at every step, without any explicit signal of what has changed. In closed-loop agent, such misreads do not end with the current prediction: the executed action changes the environment and feeds back into the observation and history of the next step, allowing errors to compound over time. We refer to this compounding failure as Sequential Distraction. The most intuitive remedy is to perform subtraction on the inputs. This is exactly what existing methods attempt: cropping parts of the current screen to retain only candidate regions of interest (Lu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b; Cheng et al., 2024). However, this strategy of giving less fundamentally misaligns with the nature of streaming interaction in two ways. First, the decisive signal could emerge from audio, video, or device status at any moment, channels entirely outside the scope of spatial cropping. Second, even when the signal resides on the screen, the crudely cropped background often contains the essential contextual evidence needed to ground accurate coordinates and text parameters. The problem is not that the decoder is given too much, but that it lacks guidance on how to prioritize it. proper focus mechanism should change how the decoder reads the observation, rather than altering what it is given. We realize this principle in FocusGUI  (Fig. 2)  . Since the decoder can already read the full observation and what it lacks is signal of what matters at the current step, FocusGUI leaves both the backbone and its input untouched and supplies that signal alongside them. At every step, it exposes the observation as separable perceptual channels, scores each against reference derived from the current observation as whole, and compresses the prioritized channels into compact focus latent. The latent enters as zero-initialized residual at the boundary where the decoder begins to generate the action. This residual reallocates attention over the entire observation without altering it, guiding both the choice of action and the grounding of its arguments. Training uses next-action supervision alone, with no labels indicating which modality matters. On average across four omni-modal backbones, FocusGUI raises Type Match from 31.0% to 64.2% and Exact Match from 11.2% to 33.5% over the frozen backbone, and reaches 1.9 the Type Match of the strongest enhancement method. The gains grow with interaction depth, as Sequential Distraction predicts: from the first step to the fourth, the frozen Qwen2.5-Omni loses half of its Type Match while FocusGUI retains 86.8%. Our contributions are as follows: An empirical account of Sequential Distraction: in multi-step omni-modal GUI interaction, relevance is step-level property, transient across steps and sparse within them, and because actions re-enter the observation, per-step misreads compound into trajectory drift. 2 Focused Omni-Modal GUI Agents Figure 2 FocusGUI. The frozen backbones original pathway is left intact (top). From the same observation, FocusGUI exposes perceptual channels, scores them against decision reference recomputed at every step, compresses the result into compact focus latent, and adds it as zero-initialized residual at the positions preceding the action boundary. distinction between the evidence an agent is given and the way its decoder reads it, showing why spatial refinement cannot satisfy both the selection of an action and the grounding of its arguments, and deriving from this the form solution must take. FocusGUI, zero-initialized residual adapter at the action boundary of frozen backbone, trained from action supervision alone, whose gains across four backbones and five task categories are distributed as the account predicts.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: 3.1 Experimental Setup Dataset and Metrics. We evaluate on OmniGUI (Henry et al., 2026), benchmark of omni-modal smartphone GUI interactions across 29 applications; we use 708 episodes with 2,572 action steps. Each step pairs screenshot with synchronous audio, video, and action history, so the decisive signal can come from any of the four streams. We report Type Match (TM), Exact Match (EM), and Goal Progress (GP). TM checks whether the predicted action primitive matches the ground truth; EM further requires predicted coordinates to fall within the target elements bounding box and generated text to match the reference. GP is the fraction of correctly executed steps per episode, averaged across episodes. 5 Focused Omni-Modal GUI Agents Models. We evaluate four representative open-source omni-modal backbones: Qwen2.5Omni (Xu et al., 2025), VITA-1.5 (Fu et al., 2025), MiniCPM-o 4.5 (Cui et al., 2026), and Baichuan-Omni-1.5 (Li et al., 2025b). The four backbones support textual, visual, auditory, and temporal inputs but differ in architecture and multimodal representation, which lets the comparison probe the generality of FocusGUI across backbone families. For each backbone, the base model stays frozen, and training updates only the lightweight FocusGUI head and action predictors, using the same episode-disjoint split across all four models. Baselines. We compare against four methods, each applied to all four backbones without modifying their weights. DRS-GUI (Liu et al., 2026b), OmniParser (Lu et al., 2024), and RegionFocus (Luo et al., 2025) refine the visual input at inference by searching over candidate regions, parsing the screenshot into structured elements, and zooming into attended regions. GUI-Actor (Wu et al., 2025a) instead learns an action head over the backbones visual tokens, trained on the same annotations and split as FocusGUI with the backbone frozen. All methods receive the same observation and decoding procedure, differing only in how that observation is organized before the action is generated. The trained head separates two explanations for any gain: trainable parameters on this data, which GUI-Actor also has, and step-adaptive organization, which FocusGUI adds. Implementation Details. Evidence channels are projected into shared 128-dimensional space and weighted by the full-modal query with softmax temperature τ = 1.0; the weighted representation is compressed to 64-dimensional action-sufficient embedding and expanded into = 4 zero-initialized residual tokens added to the last four prompt embeddings before the action boundary, introducing 1.15M1.45M trainable parameters depending on the backbone. With the encoder, decoder, and LM head frozen, we train only these modules for three epochs with AdamW under the teacher-forced action-token negative log-likelihood, selecting the learning rate 2 104 and weight decay 103. At inference, the frozen decoder generates actions autoregressively with greedy decoding. Additional implementation details are provided in the Appendix D. 3.2 Main Results Consistent gains across backbones. Table 1 evaluates four omni-modal backbones under identical frozen weights. Averaged across them, FocusGUI adds 33.2 TM, 22.3 EM, and 6.6 GP points over direct inference and 30.1, 23.6, and 8.0 points over the strongest baseline at each backbone. It holds the best TM and the best EM in all 24 backbone-category cells. Why screen refinement backfires. The baselines fail in way that is diagnostic rather than incidental. DRS-GUI, OmniParser, and RegionFocus are near-neutral on TM (+0.9 points on average) yet lower EM by 28% and GP by 35% in relative terms, in 12 of 12 cases for each metric. Narrowing screenshot makes the action primitive more salient, which is what TM rewards, while discarding the surrounding context that fixes coordinates and text, which is what EM requires. None of the three reaches audio, video, or device state, so decision resting on those channels stays unrecoverable however the screen is processed. This is what our framing predicts: once relevance is property of step rather than of region, refining the region cannot restore it and may cost more than it returns. Where the gains come from. The structure of the gains indicates what the representation supplies. Per-category TM gains run from 37.3 points on Temporal, where the decisive signal persists across frames and single screenshot serves worst, to 27.8 on Instant, where the decision is reactive and largely present on the current screen; EM follows the same order. Across backbones, the overall TM spread narrows from 35.6 points to 13.0, indicating that choosing the correct primitive becomes substantially less backbone-dependent under better-organized observation. EM variation instead reflects backbone-specific argumentgeneration capacity. At episode level, improvements in per-step prediction translate into Goal Progress when they are sustained across the trajectory. Episode progress is gated by the weakest step in trajectory. Overall Type Match falls by 0.51, 1.20, 4.27, and 5.39 points when action-sufficient projection, residual alignment, step-adaptive prioritization, and channel decomposition are removed, but GP falls by 1.38, 5.38, 5.93, and 5.29 points on base roughly quarter as large. In relative terms, every component is worth four to five times more to episode progress than to single-step action type: at most 7.5% of TM against up to 33.9% of GP. Their disproportionately larger effect on GP shows that the components primarily keep trajectory from unravelling, which is what Sequential Distraction predicts. GP reveals contributions beyond TM. Decomposing the observation into channels without prioritizing them raises Type Match by 1.12 and Exact Match by 2.78 points over single integrated channel. Prioritization converts this richer channel access into episode-level stability by deciding which channel to trust. Residual alignment shows the same metric asymmetry more sharply: replacing the additive residual with prompt-embedding substitution reduces EM by 5.30 and GP by 5.38 points, compared with 1.20-point TM change. Preserving the original prompt embeddings therefore matters most for grounding the selected action primitive into correct arguments. 3.4 Performance Across Interaction Depth Sequential Distraction predicts that interference accumulates. method that suppresses it should separate from the backbone as trajectory lengthens, whereas uniformly stronger predictor would hold constant margin. sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: 4.1 GUI Agents in Omni-Modal Environments GUI agents interact with digital environments by repeatedly translating user intentions and interface observations into executable actions. Research across mobile, web, and desktop platforms has established this perceptionaction loop and progressively extended it from isolated grounding decisions to long-horizon interaction (Rawles et al., 2023; Deng et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026b). Most agents nevertheless organize their observation around the current screenshot, with previous actions or screens retained as auxiliary context. Temporal GUI benchmarks broaden this view by requiring agents to understand dynamic visual content (Jang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2025), while OmniGUI further places each action within an interleaved observation of screen, video, audio, and interaction history (Henry et al., 2026). These developments shift GUI interaction from processing sequence of interfaces to acting over an evolving omni-modal state. In parallel, omni-modal foundation models increasingly support unified or streaming perception of text, vision, and audio (Xu et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026). Broader evaluations of real-time assistants similarly emphasize online processing and continuity as multimodal events unfold (Lu et al., 2026). Such capabilities determine what model can receive; how an agent should organize that evidence for the next GUI action remains open. The closest observation-side approach augments computer-use agents with gated keyframes, audio transcription, and persistent visual narration (Li & Shi, 2026). FocusGUI addresses the complementary problem inside an omni-modal agent: given the complete observation, it learns which evidence should shape the current action and how to deliver that evidence to frozen decoder. 4.2 Perception and Grounding for GUI Agents Perception is central to GUI agents because an instruction must ultimately be connected to an actionable interface element. One line of work strengthens this connection through GUI-specific representation learning and large-scale grounding data (Cheng et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Gou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025b); another exposes explicit interface structure to general-purpose models through screen parsing (Lu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026a; Fu et al., 2026). Recent visual agents also reduce redundant screen tokens while jointly learning grounding and action generation (Lin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c). Together, these Focused Omni-Modal GUI Agents methods improve how an agent understands the current interface and determines where an action should be executed. complementary direction makes perception selective. Rather than processing the full screenshot uniformly, visual search and test-time refinement narrow the observation to promising regions (Li et al., 2025a; Luo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026d); active perception methods further decide when and how to crop, zoom, shift, or expand the visual field (Chen et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b). These approaches demonstrate the value of suppressing irrelevant interface content, but their primary control axis remains spatial: they determine which part of the current screen deserves closer inspection (Zhang et al., 2026a). Omni-modal interaction introduces an additional axis, since relevance also changes across information sources and action steps. FocusGUI extends focused perception from spatial localization to step-dependent representation construction over the complete observation, complementing existing GUI grounding mechanisms.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We identify Sequential Distraction as primary challenge in multi-step omni-modal GUI interaction, where unfiltered observations can lead to compounding errors due to transient and sparse relevance. To address this, we formulate the concept of Focused Perception and implement it through FocusGUI, lightweight adapter that dynamically prioritizes perceptual channels, compresses them into an action-sufficient latent, and delivers the result via zero-initialized residual at the action boundary. This method relies solely on action annotations and leaves the underlying backbone completely frozen. Evaluations across four backbones demonstrate that FocusGUI substantially improves Type Match over existing enhancement methods and maintains high accuracy at deeper interaction steps where historical context typically degrades. While our current prioritization depends on the present observation, future work could extend this mechanism to anticipate channel relevance, which may help mitigate trajectory drift earlier in the interaction sequence.

sections.title: B Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: FocusGUI is designed as lightweight mechanism for improving how frozen omni-modal GUI agents organize step-dependent evidence, and it is complementary to advances in perception, grounding, and planning. Our current formulation computes channel priorities from the observation available at each interaction step, which keeps the method simple and model-agnostic; extending this mechanism to incorporate anticipatory signals about which evidence may become important in subsequent steps is natural direction for future work. Our experiments span four omni-modal backbones and five interaction categories; extending focused perception to broader computer-use settings is natural next step.

sections.title: F Case Study
sections.content: To demonstrate the comprehensiveness and robustness of FocusGUI across diverse interaction paradigms, we present two distinct case studies encompassing both cross-modal temporal reasoning and multi-step semantic localization. Real-world GUI operation requires agents to seamlessly transition between different cognitive modes: some tasks demand patient monitoring of streaming sensory inputs (e.g., waiting for an auditory cue), while others require precise, sequential spatial navigation through dense interfaces. The following examples illustrate how FocusGUI successfully navigates these contrasting extremes by dynamically prioritizing relevant perceptual channels. Figure 11 highlights scenario where the decisive signal is entirely auditory and temporal, requiring the agent to ignore static visual saliency until specific semantic condition is met. Conversely, Figure 12 showcases highly spatial and semantic task, where the agent must execute precise sequence of UI interactions (opening filters, selecting specific nested options) based on composite text instruction. Together, these cases confirm that FocusGUIs step-adaptive prioritization effectively generalizes across fundamentally different types of GUI challenges, preventing Sequential Distraction in both streaming and structurally complex environments. 21 Focused Omni-Modal GUI Agents Figure 11 Case study on cross-modal temporal reasoning. The agent is instructed to pause video based on specific auditory cues ("past/history/childhood"). The visual interface remains largely static, forcing the model to rely on streaming audio comprehension over multiple steps. FocusGUI successfully avoids premature visual actions, dynamically shifting priority to the audio channel and executing the spatial action (tapping pause) precisely when the semantic condition is met. Figure 12 Case study on multi-step semantic planning and spatial localization. The agent executes complex sequence of interface interactions based on detailed text instruction. It successfully navigates through dynamic UI changeslocating small filter icon, understanding the popup menu, and sequentially selecting "Like count", "Liked", and "This Week".
